claim: A tournament on 52 vertices has property S_4 if and only if, for every vertex v, the subtournament induced by the in-neighbourhood of v has property S_3. Equivalently, no tournament on 52 vertices has S_4 if and only if every tournament on 52 vertices has at least one vertex whose induced in-neighbourhood fails S_3. Iterating the same identity, S_4 fails if and only if there is a sequence of m ≤ 4 vertices in which each later vertex beats every earlier one and no vertex beats the whole sequence. The equivalence does not show that either side is true, and it does not solve Erdős problem 902.
definitions: A tournament is an oriented complete graph with no loops: for distinct u and v, exactly one of u → v and v → u holds. N^-(v) is the set of vertices that beat v, and T[U] is the induced subtournament on U. For X ⊆ V, D(X) is the set of vertices outside X that beat every member of X. The empty subtournament has γ = 0. For a tournament U on m vertices and an integer k ≥ 1, γ(U) is the size of a smallest dominating set: a set D such that every vertex outside D is beaten by some vertex of D. The whole vertex set dominates, so γ(U) ≤ m when m ≥ 1, and γ of the empty tournament is 0. Property S_k means m ≥ k + 1 and every k-subset has nonempty dominator set. In particular S_3 on an induced in-neighbourhood is a statement about that subtournament alone: the dominator of a triple must lie inside the in-neighbourhood. The order 52 is at least 4 and the vertex set is nonempty. No hypothesis is placed on degrees, regularity, tightness, or on f(3).
argument:
The argument proves three lemmas and then specialises them to order 52. It does not assume Lemma S1, Lemma I, Lemma J, or the value of f(3).

Lemma A, the domination form. Let U be any tournament, possibly empty, and let k ≥ 1. Then γ(U) > k if and only if U has S_k.

First suppose γ(U) > k. Then m = |V(U)| ≥ γ(U) ≥ k + 1. Let X be a k-subset. If D(X) were empty, every vertex y outside X would fail to beat some member of X, hence would be beaten by some member of X, and X would be a dominating set of size k. That would force γ(U) ≤ k. So D(X) is nonempty and U has S_k.

Conversely, suppose U has S_k, so m ≥ k + 1 and every k-subset has a dominator. If γ(U) ≤ k, choose a dominating set D of that size and enlarge it to a k-subset X. The enlargement is possible because m ≥ k + 1 and |D| ≤ k. The set X still dominates. A vertex outside X that beat every member of X would be unbeaten by D. So D(X) is empty, contradicting S_k. Thus γ(U) > k.

Both directions cover the small orders. If m ≤ k, then γ(U) ≤ m ≤ k, so γ(U) > k is false, and S_k is false because it requires m ≥ k + 1. The empty tournament has γ = 0, so it fails γ > k for every k ≥ 1, and it fails S_k.

Lemma B, the recurrence. Let T be a nonempty tournament. Then γ(T) = 1 + min_v γ(T[N^-(v)]).

For an arbitrary vertex v, let U = N^-(v) and let D' be a minimum dominating set of T[U]. The set {v} ∪ D' dominates T. Every vertex of N^+(v) is beaten by v. Every vertex of U outside D' is beaten by some vertex of D'. There is nothing else in V(T). Hence γ(T) ≤ 1 + γ(T[U]). Taking the minimum over v gives γ(T) ≤ 1 + min_v γ(T[N^-(v)]).

For the matching lower bound, suppose some v satisfied γ(T[N^-(v)]) ≤ γ(T) − 2. The preceding paragraph would give γ(T) ≤ 1 + γ(T[N^-(v)]) ≤ γ(T) − 1, which is impossible. Domination numbers are integers, so every in-neighbourhood has domination number at least γ(T) − 1. Therefore the minimum is at least γ(T) − 1, and 1 plus the minimum is at least γ(T). Combined with the upper bound, both inequalities are equalities.

Lemma C, one deletion. Let T be nonempty and let k ≥ 1. Then γ(T) > k if and only if every vertex v satisfies γ(T[N^-(v)]) > k − 1.

This is Lemma B: γ(T) = 1 + min γ(in), so the left side exceeds k exactly when the minimum exceeds k − 1, which, because the values are integers and the minimum is attained, is exactly the condition that every in-neighbourhood has domination number greater than k − 1.

Application to S_4. Let T be a tournament on 52 vertices. By Lemma A with k = 4, T has S_4 if and only if γ(T) > 4. By Lemma C, this holds if and only if every in-neighbourhood has domination number greater than 3. By Lemma A applied inside each induced in-neighbourhood, with k = 3, that condition is exactly S_3 on every induced in-neighbourhood. An empty or small in-neighbourhood fails both γ > 3 and S_3, so those vertices are not an extra case.

Therefore T has S_4 if and only if every induced in-neighbourhood has S_3. Negating both sides, and using that a tournament on 52 vertices has at least one vertex, gives the stated formulation: no tournament on 52 vertices has S_4 if and only if every such tournament has a vertex whose induced in-neighbourhood fails S_3.

The same step iterated. Apply Lemma C three further times inside the successive in-neighbourhoods. For a nonempty tournament, γ ≤ 4 if and only if there exist m ≤ 4 and distinct vertices x_1, ..., x_m such that x_j beats x_i whenever i < j, and no vertex beats every one of x_1, ..., x_m.

The sequence produces a dominating set of size m: the later-to-earlier rule makes {x_1, ..., x_m} a transitive subtournament, and a vertex outside the sequence that was unbeaten by all of it would beat all of it. Conversely, if γ ≤ 4, Lemma B supplies a vertex x whose in-neighbourhood has domination number at most 3, and induction on that subtournament supplies the rest of a sequence of length at most 4. The empty sequence is allowed only for the empty tournament, which is excluded at order 52; a transmitter is the sequence of length 1. On 52 vertices, γ ≤ 4 is exactly the failure of S_4, by Lemma A. This is the same equivalence, written without naming an induced copy of S_3.

The number 52 is used only as an order at which the tournament is nonempty and has at least four vertices, so that Lemma A applies to S_4. The same proof gives the identical reduction at every order N ≥ 4.

evidence.hand_proof: Lemmas A, B and C are proved in the argument from the definitions. No identity from LEMMAS.md is used.
evidence.recurrence_enumeration: All labelled tournaments on 1 through 6 vertices were checked: 33867 tournaments. In every one, the domination number equals 1 plus the minimum of the domination numbers of the induced in-neighbourhoods.
evidence.tower_enumeration: All labelled tournaments on 0 through 5 vertices were checked: 1100 tournaments. For each k from 0 through 4, the domination number is at most k if and only if a sequence of length at most k exists in which each later vertex beats every earlier vertex and no vertex beats the whole sequence.
evidence.property_enumeration: For k in {1, 2, 3} and every labelled tournament on 1 through 6 vertices, S_k holds if and only if every induced in-neighbourhood has S_{k-1}. The empty tournament is the only mismatch, and only because a universal quantifier over its vertex set is vacuously true; order 52 is nonempty. Among these checks, 27362 pairs (k, tournament) had S_k, so the positive side was tested.
evidence.paley_checks: In the Paley tournament of order 7, with an edge i → j when j − i is a nonzero quadratic residue, S_2 holds and all seven induced in-neighbourhoods have S_1, while S_3 fails and those in-neighbourhoods fail S_2. In the Paley tournament of order 19 the same rule gives S_3, and all nineteen induced in-neighbourhoods, each of order 9, have S_2.
evidence.what_was_not_checked: No tournament on 52 vertices was enumerated. The enumeration does not bear on existence.

weaknesses: The status proved applies only to the equivalence. Neither side has been established: the report does not show that every tournament on 52 vertices has a vertex whose in-neighbourhood fails S_3, and it does not show that an S_4 tournament on 52 vertices exists. Erdős problem 902 is not solved. The order of f(n) is untouched, and so is the upper bound f(4) ≤ 67. The identity holds at every order at least 4, so the number 52 plays no special role. Granting the classical theorem f(3) = 19, which is not re-proved here, would dispose only of a vertex of in-degree at most 18. Every remaining case has all in-degrees at least 19, and an in-neighbourhood of that order can carry S_3. The sequence form allows length strictly less than 4. It is not the assertion that some transitive 4-set is undominated; a shorter transitive dominating set need not extend to a transitive dominating 4-set. Lemma S1, the tight-pair bound J ≥ 3, and the case split J = 3, 4 were not used.
